items.title: What it took to make images load faster on Reddit Android
items.summary: Written by Merve Karaman and Aleksei Bykov  The problem we set out to solve On Reddit Android, image posts account for roughly one in three post views on both the Home feed and Post Detail, the screen where users view a post and its comments. Images are the most-viewed post type on each surface. When images load too slowly, users may scroll past or leave the screen before they become visible. Those exits hurt our image-loading service-level objective (SLO), our target for images appearing successfully while users are still there to see them.  To users, an image post looked the same on Home and Post Detail. Under the hood, though, the two screens used separate code to render images and track their performance, and they did not always request the same image URL. These differences, along with inconsistent cache behavior, made optimizations harder to apply to both screens. They also meant an image already loaded in the feed could be downloaded again when the user opened the post. We set out to make images appear sooner and more reliably, while building a shared image-loading foundation for Home and Post Detail. Across the initiative, user-level p90 image-loading latency fell by 37.3% on Post Detail and 10.7% on Home. Measuring whether images actually got better During these experiments, we measured image-loading performance at two levels. At the user level, we calculated each user’s p90 successful image-loading time, then took the 90th percentile across those values. At the event level, we calculated the 90th percentile across all successful image loads. The first gives each user equal weight; the second gives each image load equal weight. Unless otherwise noted, p90 latency results below are reported at the user level.  Successful-load latency also leaves out failures and images users never stayed long enough to see. When a fix turns a failed load into a slow successful load, it adds a slow sample to the latency distribution. P90 can therefore increase even as reliability improves. We evaluated latency alongside load success, exits before visibility, and SLO attainment to understand whether images actually got better. What shipped and why it helped Prefetching at the right time Reddit Android already prefetched images and videos before users reached them. As we discussed in our previous post on video performance, fetching content earlier can reduce waiting, but aggressive prefetching can slow competing requests. During this initiative, we refined our existing image prefetching in feeds, extended it to notifications and cold-start deeplinks, and added bandwidth gating for constrained connections.  Where to prefetch: Our existing prefetching loaded one item past the last visible post. We tested distances of one to five items ahead of it. We also tried anchoring on the first visible item, but how far it reached past the screen depended on post height, so we kept the last visible item as the anchor. When to prefetch: When a new page of feed items arrived, we checked whether its first item was within our prefetch window. If so, we prefetched images for its first three items, then continued prefetching as users scrolled. We skipped this step on initial load and refresh to avoid competing with the feed’s own requests. Choosing the distance: We selected a three-item distance, which reduced p90 image-loading latency by 6.1% for image posts on Home. It also reduced by 24.7% the rate of exits where users waited more than 150 ms but left before the image appeared. Fetching farther ahead produced larger latency gains, but three items consumed less bandwidth and had fewer comment-loading failures than the four-item variant.  Figure 1: We extended prefetching from one item past the screen to three.  On Reddit, ranking determines which posts appear in a feed and in what order. The resulting mix of content can affect prefetching performance, so the same prefetching distance may not work equally well across feeds. We plan to test prefetching rules tailored to different ranking scenarios, but have not yet evaluated this approach.  We also gave images a head start before users entered Post Detail. For trending push notifications, we prefetched post data and media when the notification arrived, reducing successful-image-load p90 on Post Detail by 10.9%. For cold-start deeplinks, we began fetching earlier during app startup, before the UI was ready. This reduced the time until users could interact with Post Detail by 2.9%.  These speculative requests shared bandwidth with images already on screen and videos being played. On constrained connections, fetching upcoming content could delay what users were currently trying to see. We added bandwidth gating to skip feed image prefetching below an estimated 5 Mbps. The app smooths bandwidth estimates supplied with image responses; when no estimate is available, prefetching continues.
